Title: r - Minimum sample size required in paired t-tests and statistic significance - Cross Validated
# Minimum sample size required in paired t-tests and statistic significance. Is a sample size of 50 enough for the paired t-tests? I saw this post What is a minimum sample size for a paired t-test and what is a non-parametric equivalent if data is non-normal?, but my questions remains. Another question that is bothering me is why are sample sizes in paired t-tests much lower when comparing to tests like two-way ANOVA (for example)? For both of them, since I only got 150 machines, I guess my sample size is predefined, but how can I ensure that my tests will have significance, i.e, 95% confidence and a certain margin of errors? If the question is how big a sample size do you need for the Central Limit Theorem to allow you to use normal based tests like the paired-t when the population is not normal? If your question is the minimum sample size to have a certain power to detect a given effect size, then this really depends on the effect size that you want to see and how much variation you expect (the standard deviation of the differences). You also ask why paired tests require smaller sample sizes than unpaired. In your case you are going to have household to household variation (a family of 4 will likely consume much more water than a single person), in a non-paired study that household to household variation will be included in the residual standard deviation, but proper pairing will remove/adjust for most of the household to household variation, so the paired sample size calculation will be based on a much smaller standard deviation than the unpaired equivalent. According to what I have learned there is no minimum sample size for a t-test. In fact the t-test is suitable for cases where the $n$ sample size is: 3 and more. A paired t-test on observations $\{X\_{1i}\}\_{i=1}^n$ and $\{X\_{2i}\}\_{i=1}^n$ **is the same** as a one-sample t test on differences. ### why are sample sizes in paired t-tests much lower when comparing to tests like two-way ANOVA (for example)? Is a sample size of 50 enough for the paired t-tests?

results.content: What are some examples where we use confidence intervals instead of significance tests (with or without small samples)? We use confidence intervals when estimating and we use significance tests when doing hypothesis tests. We use confidence intervals when estimating and we use significance tests when doing hypothesis tests. How do you model different results of significance tests and confidence limits for the same data (hypothesis testing, statistical significance, confidence interval, statistics)? What is the simplest explanation of hypothesis testing, p value, significance level, and confidence interval? A Confidence interval is an interval estimate, a range of values that could plausibly include the true/unknown population mean mu, set up using information from the sample (N, mean M, standard deviation SD). * If a hypothesized value of mu does not lie within the 95% CI you set up for your sample data, then a null hypothesis significance test using alpha = .05, two-tailed, will lead to decision to reject H0. * If a hypothesized value of mu does lie within the 95% CI you set up for your sample data, then a null hypothesis significance test using alpha = .05, two-tailed, will lead to decision not to reject H0. We can test that assumption by measuring temperature for a sample of people, setting up a 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the mean of that sample, and asking whether that CI does or does not include 98.6. results.title: statistical significance - Sign test: p and CI contradiction (significant but CI includes 0 AND not significant but CI doesn't include 0) - Cross Validated
results.content:
Title: statistical significance - Sign test: p and CI contradiction (significant but CI includes 0 AND not significant but CI doesn't include 0) - Cross Validated
I run a sign test in R and get repeatedly contradicting p-values and confidence interval (CI). It is well known (but maybe not that well, unfortunately) that the Sign test does not handle zero’s (values equal to the hypothesized median) properly. This is a similar approach to what one does for two one sided tests (TOST), but here we are really doing TOSp (Two one sided p-values; computing 2 1-tailed p-values, summing them, and then running a single test against our $\alpha$). So we should get the same p-value with this TOSp approach as with a 2-tailed Sign test (which is nothing more than a 2-tailed binomial test). A binomial test or a Sign test will give the same $p=0.064909$. Note that the BDSA::SIGN.test returns the exact same p-value as before, which certainly does not feel right. The observed median is now 2.5 (still closer to 0), and the p-value is greater, in line with expectations (while the BDSA::SIGN.test still returns the exact same p-value). Note that [-1,15] is exactly the CI which SIGN.test gives as its “Upper achieved CI” (but it does not exclude the bounds, which it should, because the binomial test rejects these 2 possible values of the median!). The BDSA::Sign.test does not compute p-values correctly when zero’s (values equal to the hypothesized median) are present in the data set. And compute CI’s using binomial tests and using TOSp (because you will have at least 1 zero there...). My binomial test approach for median=0 in x2 gives $p=0.06491$ (testing Binomial $P=0.5$ based on 18 successes out of 50), which agrees with your p-value. Using x1 as example, there are 20 out of 50 instances of $X\le 0$, and a one-sided Binomial test gives $p=0.1013$. There are 40 out of 50 instances of $X\ge 0$, and a one-sided Binomial test gives $p\approx 1$. In order to have a two-sided test of $\nu=0$, I use Bonferroni to combine the p-values, i.e., minimum p-value times 2 (this is in line with the standard construction of two-sided tests in symmetric situations), giving $p=0.2026$, which happens to be equal to the p-value of the two-sided Binomial test for 20 out of 50.
